sections.title: Reading Passage 1 — Traditional houses in Bhutan
sections.passage:
Traditional houses in Bhutan

The Kingdom of Bhutan is located high up at the eastern edge of the Himalayas in Southern Asia. Traditional architecture there has evolved over many centuries to suit the local environment, climate, available materials, technology, and more significantly, cultural traditions and spiritual beliefs. Spaces in traditional Bhutanese homes are designed to be functional yet flexible. A traditional house has three main floors and an attic, laid out in a vertical hierarchy with each level having a distinctive function. The lower ground floor space is used for sheltering livestock such as cattle and goats, with the store rooms for animal food and agricultural equipment in the middle level, and spaces in the upper level for the use of family and guests. The attic holds relics of ancestors so that the living can look after the dead – and the dead, perhaps, intercede for the living. The Bhutanese thus see their houses as miniature renderings of the universe: the lowest floor as an underworld occupied by beasts, and the top as heaven, the realm of enlightened beings and the honoured dead.

Within traditional Bhutanese building practice, the design and construction of buildings is managed by local carpenters and stone masons, who are so experienced and skilled that they can work without the use of any drawn plans. Their knowledge of timber joinery techniques also allows them to construct buildings without the use of metal bolts or screws. This is architecture without architects, without drawings or textbooks. It is the result of knowledge passed verbally from one generation of builders to the next. There is little concern for invention or novelty in the design of these buildings or in the techniques used to construct them; a building form has evolved over centuries that works, and that keeps tradition alive.

Traditional Bhutanese houses have a number of distinctive elements. The external walls are constructed of stone or rammed earth, and whitewashed in lime. They are broad and heavy at the base, while their thickness is reduced on the upper stories of the building. Animals are restricted to the lowest level, and ladders allow people to access the upper parts of the building. The main windows of the house are located in the upper stories and are surrounded by colourful wooden frames carved with intricate floral and animal images. At the top of the building there is a space covered by the sloping roof of the house with a large gap left between the roof and walls, meaning that this part of the house has particularly good ventilation. This attic is strengthened with centrally placed posts and has wooden beams which are designed to overhang the walls all around the house and protect them. The roof is covered by wooden tiles and, instead of metal nails, these are held in place by stones. To prevent these from rolling off the roof, its slope cannot be too steep. The roof often has a white prayer flag on top as a crowning feature.

The features of these houses reflect the abilities and needs of both the builders and the inhabitants. The builders of these indigenous houses did not have the necessary technology for the construction of curved walls which would reproduce the curves and slopes of the hills and valleys in the surrounding land. Instead, they created a heavy, box-like structure with straight walls that met in angular corners, but whose upper stories and roof seemed to be suspended and floating above the rest of the house. The shape of the buildings was also a response to the climatic conditions of the land. It resulted in a smaller ratio of surface area to volume, exposing less of the building to the cold outside, and conserving heat within the building. The fact that the roofs were sloping rather than flat protected the earth walls from the heavy rainfall in the monsoon season and stopped snow from settling on the roof during the winter and damaging it. In the past, the lack of refrigeration meant that food for consumption in the winter months had to be dried for preservation. This required a space that was secure, clean and well-ventilated. The attic space, with its open-roof structure, fulfilled this need, and was also a place where spiritual rituals could take place.

Although the availability of new materials such as cement and steel has led to changes in the design and structure of houses, particularly in urban areas, many of these traditional features of architecture have been maintained to the present day.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2 — The origins of language
sections.passage:
The origins of language

A   People have puzzled over the origins of language for hundreds of years. It is, after all, one of the few traits that distinguishes humans from all other animals. No other species has a communication system that comes close to it in its flexibility and range of expression.

Many scientists are now convinced that speech of some kind had emerged by at least 400,000 years ago. It may even have started hundreds of thousands of years before that, they argue, when our ancestors first began displaying more sophisticated cooperative behaviours – possibly two million years ago or more, when the use of sophisticated stone tools indicates some kind of advanced communication system.

B   Establishing exactly what pushed us along that evolutionary path has been much harder. The naturalist Charles Darwin provided one explanation. In 1871 he argued that our human ancestors developed a kind of musical protolanguage. Like bird song, these sounds had no specific meaning, but were used by males to attract mates. In this way, our vocal flexibility first emerged through sexual selection, with competing males developing more complex songs to beat their rivals.

C   But many researchers don’t accept these arguments. Instead, some point out that all humans, including those who are blind, move their hands as they talk, often without realising they are doing so. Based on this, they propose a protolanguage in which communication arose through gesture. This may have been a much easier way of communicating at the beginning of language evolution. Non-human primates can be surprisingly dextrous with their hands, but tend to find it harder to learn to reproduce specific sounds.

D   As compelling as these arguments are, they can’t explain why we made the switch to language that was primarily vocalised. That brings us to the third idea, the notion that language first emerged through onomatopoeia – imitating the sounds of things. After all, even children will mimic a horse’s neigh or a wolf’s howl. Yet historically, this option has been the least popular, thanks to a couple of seemingly insoluble problems.

First, it requires the ability to imitate sounds. Yet our early ancestors lacked the anatomical and neural adaptations needed to do this. However, it now appears that non-human primates have more breath control and vocal flexibility than was once thought, suggesting that the anatomy of our early ancestors may have meant they were capable of crude imitation.

Secondly, people claimed that onomatopoeia is too limited to form the basis of a protolanguage. How would our ancestors have signalled silent concepts, such as a particular plant or tool, or something more abstract, like directions to a river? What sound would they use to represent a quiet animal like a rabbit? But recent research suggests that inventive use of onomatopoeia can communicate a much wider range of concepts than was once imagined.

E   With so many pros and cons for each hypothesis of protolanguage, we may seem no closer to finding an answer. But what if all three ideas contain elements of truth? After all, several of the seven thousand or so languages spoken today – including some of Australia’s Aboriginal languages and Paamese in Vanuatu – use elements of all these types of communication interchangeably. So perhaps, instead of offering competing explanations, these three ideas might work together to provide a unified theory of the origin of language. That is exactly what anthropologist Jerome Lewis of University College London is now proposing.

F   Like Darwin, Lewis believes singing was the first step to using language. In place of sexual selection, however, he suggests it emerged for protection. This idea is inspired by his work with the Bayaka people in central Africa, where people take turns to sing all night to ward off predators. Similar behaviour has been found among the San people in southern Africa and Indian forest dwellers, he says.

This, in turn, would have enabled a growing talent for mimicry, which might have aided hunting. Modern hunter-gatherers often imitate the sounds of forest animals to draw their prey towards them, says Lewis. In the past, people could have used those same sounds when recounting stories based on their experiences, perhaps with the aim of passing on knowledge of hunting to younger listeners. The sounds could quickly become more structured and stylised, eventually establishing an agreed lexicon between speakers that resembled modern language.

G   Robin Dunbar at the University of Oxford also points out that singing together stimulates the production of endorphins, hormones that promote social cohesion. So it would have allowed our ancestors to live in a larger group, giving them strength in numbers and helping them to keep predators at bay.

Lewis agrees that those early musical vocalisations may have had an important social function. In his view, this also helped create the shared trust that is essential for language to take off. Words, after all, are useless unless people are using them to share interests and information.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3 — Trading and marketing in the natural world
sections.passage:
Trading and marketing in the natural world

Humans aren’t the only living creatures to carry out business deals – even fish and fungi do it

‘The propensity to barter and exchange one thing for another … is common to all men, and to be found in no other race of animals,’ wrote economist Adam Smith back in 1776. The idea that humans are the only species capable of economic behaviour seems to make sense. Responding to shifts in supply and demand, for instance, must require a brain that is highly developed and able to think through decisions rationally. Or so we thought. But it is becoming apparent that pretty much everywhere we look in nature we find evidence of surprisingly sophisticated economic decision-making. It appears that many animals and organisms make trades, and that some are surprisingly clever at it, capable of manipulating the market in their own selfish interests.

To investigate this, Redouan Bshary from the University of Neuchatel in Switzerland studied a small reef fish called the cleaner wrasse, which makes a living by nibbling tiny parasites from between the scales of other fish. He picked this wrasse because even though its behaviour is a nice example of mutual benefit, in that the cleaners get food from the parasites and the clients – the other fish – get cleaned, there is a conflict of interest. The bodies of the client fish are covered by a layer of mucus, and the cleaners can ‘cheat’, feeding on this mucus or even on the tissues of the client rather than removing the parasites. The temptation to cheat may be strong. ‘Mucus seems to be quite energy rich and cleaners do not have to search for it, while they have to search for parasites,’ says Bshary. That means to get good service, these clients have to get cleaners to go against their preference.

Having learned to scuba-dive, Bshary spent countless hours observing cleaner wrasse in the Red Sea. He saw that they have two types of client. There are visitor fish, such as parrotfish, which can grow 40 centimetres long and can travel easily, giving them access to several cleaner wrasse, and there are resident fish, like the smaller melanurus wrasse, that tend to stick to one cleaner. Bshary figured that visitors had a strategic advantage because they could shop around and switch cleaners if they weren’t satisfied. Sure enough, he found that these clients were seen more quickly than resident fish and treated more gently, with the cleaners less likely to sneak a bite of their mucus layer.

The cunning adjustments to the coral reef free market don’t end there. Most recently, observing around Lizard Island in Australia, Bshary and his colleagues noticed that cleaner wrasse had stopped giving priority access to visitor fish. The reason, he suggests, is that adverse weather conditions had killed off 80 per cent of the cleaner wrasse. It had suddenly become a restricted market. Cleaners were in short supply, and they made the most of this. There was nothing to stop them from making visitors wait.

‘I was optimistic that the market paradigm would work in this system,’ says Bshary. ‘But the sophistication continues to surprise me. These fish are constantly adjusting to market conditions and updating their strategies accordingly. That they can do so with tiny brains challenges the idea that only creatures with weighty lumps of grey matter are capable of complex behaviour such as responding to shifts in supply and demand. We are probably going to have to rethink that. We now see that, at least within ecologically relevant contexts, pretty much any animal can show high levels of sophistication in terms of their behaviour.’

In one of the most recently studied examples of biological trading, the traders don’t have brains at all. Toby Kiers, an evolutionary biologist at the Free University Amsterdam, studies mycorrhizal fungi, which have a mutually beneficial association with plant roots, providing phosphorus to the roots and receiving carbon in return. This type of trading is the perfect environment for market dynamics to emerge, she says, because a single fungal network can be connected to many plants and so can switch between trading partners rapidly. The plants in turn can choose from many competing fungal strains.

Kiers and her colleagues carried out a series of experiments in which a fungus was connected to several hosts at once. One thing they found is that the fungus will avoid trading with plants growing in the shade. ‘The fungi are avoiding bad trading partners,’ she says. But that is far from the fungi’s most cunning trick. Kiers has also caught them hoarding resources, storing their phosphorus in a form that is inaccessible to the plants. ‘In doing so, they can artificially inflate the price, getting more carbon in return from the plants,’ she says. ‘It’s a brilliant strategy.’

Still, animals, plants and fungi can’t match the complexity of humans’ economic behaviour. As far as we know, they don’t employ a common currency, for instance. But that can make them all the more revealing. ‘While primates are undoubtedly more interesting to watch, fungal-plant systems can be precisely manipulated and trades can be tracked,’ says Kiers. ‘We can watch trade strategies evolve, study tipping points for when and how trade relationships break down.’

For Kiers, the most interesting thing about studying these fungi is that it reveals trading strategies uncontaminated by cognition. ‘These are pure economic decisions, nothing to do with resentment or hope or anything like that,’ she says. ‘Here we can witness economic behaviour in its most pure and ancestral form’.
